discovers, develops, manufactures and delivers innovative medicines to fight some of the world’s toughest diseases. Harnessing the best of biology and technology, Amgen reaches millions of patients with its medicines, helping make people’s lives easier, fuller and longer. More than 45 years ago, Amgen helped establish the biotechnology industry at its U.S. headquarters in Thousand Oaks, California, and it remains at the cutting edge of innovation, using technology and human genetic data to push beyond what is known today. Amgen is advancing a broad and deep pipeline and portfolio of medicines to treat heart disease, obesity and obesity-related conditions, rare diseases, inflammatory conditions and cancer. Amgen has been consistently recognized for innovation and workplace culture, including honors from Fast Company and Forbes . Amgen is one of the 30 companies that comprise the Dow Jones Industrial Average ® , and it is also part of the Nasdaq-100 Index ® , which includes the largest and most innovative non-financial companies listed on the Nasdaq Stock Market based on market capitalization. The Rhythm of Life Watch Video Reaching Seriously Ill Patients Worldwide We have a presence in approximately 100 countries worldwide and our innovative medicines have reached millions of people in the fight against serious illnesses. We focus on four therapeutic areas, general medicine, rare disease, inflammation, and oncology, delivering innovative medicines to help make people's lives easier, fuller and longer. Investing in Science and Innovation We pursue new ways to do science using tools like AI, generative biology and human data to discover what is not yet known and develop new precision medicines to fight the world’s toughest diseases. Making Medicines Safely and Reliably Many of Amgen's medicines are made through a highly complex process involving living cells. We aim to deliver for "every patient, every time", and we have a long-running reputation for the reliability of our supply chain. Operating Responsibly Making a positive difference in the world is at the heart of what we do at Amgen — and it goes beyond making vital medicines. We also help build a better world by focusing on environmental, social and governance issues that matter most to our business and our stakeholders. DOWNLOADS Amgen Fact Sheet In This Section Letter to Our Shareholders The capabilities we are building across science, technology, and manufacturing are enabling us to move faster, operate more efficiently, and reach more patients than ever before. With a diversified portfolio, strong commercial performance, and a deep and advancing pipeline, we are executing on our strategy to deliver meaningful innovation for patients and attractive long-term growth for shareholders. Read 2025 Letter to Shareholders Mission and Values Amgen strives to serve patients by transforming the promise of science and biotechnology into therapies that have the power to restore health or save lives. Leadership As one of the early pioneers of the biotech industry, Amgen's innovative and inspirational leadership is a core part of our social architecture. Senior Management Board of Directors Scientific Advisory Boards Brand Partners By partnering with organizations that share our commitment to improving people's lives, we're helping bring science to new audiences, strengthen communities, and extend the impact of research beyond the lab. Therapy Areas At Amgen, we are committed to delivering innovative medicines in four key therapeutic areas: general medicine, rare diseases, inflammation, and oncology. How We Operate At Amgen, we are relentless in applying the highest ethical standards to everything we do. Corporate Governance Business Ethics and Compliance Policies Practices and Disclosures Awards and Accolades Amgen has been the recipient of numerous awards and accolades over the years, ranging from recognition of our pioneering science and innovation, philanthropy and corporate social responsibility to our commitment to being a great place to work. Amgen History A biotechnology innovator since 1980, Amgen has grown to be one of the world's leading independent biotechnology companies and has reached millions of patients around the world. across R&D to accelerate drug discovery and clinical development, helping us move from molecule to medicine with speed and efficiency. AI supports our study of vast amounts of omics data to better understand human and disease biology, generate deep insights into why therapies work and find ways we can improve and maximize their potential across various therapeutic areas. As we advance potential treatments through clinical trials, we use AI to increase trial efficiency and improve success rates. By analyzing both omics and real-world data we can optimize trial protocols, identify successful trial sites and eligible patients. AI and data science are helping us deliver more effective advancements, faster than ever before. Pediatric Cancer Research > RESPONSIBILITY 07.25.2026 Why MrBeast, Stand Up To Cancer, and Amgen Joined Forces to Support Pediatric Cancer Research The world's biggest YouTuber is using his platform to bring hope to children living with cancer. Here's how Amgen is helping advance the research behind that hope. Beast Philanthropy , the charitable organization founded by Jimmy Donaldson (also known globally as MrBeast , the world's largest content creator), joins Stand Up To Cancer , and Amgen to create a global awareness and fundraising effort that aims to accelerate research and the next generation of breakthroughs for cancers affecting children, adolescents, and young adults. The collaboration also supports the launch of a Stand Up To Cancer Pediatric Cancer Dream Team, a new research project dedicated to advancing discoveries for children with cancer. Donaldson's latest video "I Helped 100 Kids Fight Cancer" may be one of his most meaningful, as he's joined by LeBron James, Dr. Mike, and others to grant wishes for 100 children living with cancer. Explaining why LeBron and his foundation chose to get involved, a spokesperson said, "We all know someone who's been impacted by cancer, so this is something that resonates for all of us. The LeBron James Family Foundation works to uplift people in any way we can, so to be part of such a tremendous effort with a reach of this magnitude is an honor. We can't wait for the world to see and be a part of this project." Behind every wish is something bigger. The hope created in the video begins years earlier—in laboratories, research institutions, and collaborations dedicated to changing what's possible for children living with cancer. That's where Amgen comes in. Why Research Matters Every major medical breakthrough begins with research. What happens in the laboratory today has the potential to change what happens in the doctor's office tomorrow. For more than 45 years, Amgen has invested in research to better understand disease and develop innovative medicines for patients around the world. Today, the company continues to advance research across oncology, cardiovascular disease, inflammation, rare diseases, and obesity and related conditions, with a commitment to turning scientific discovery into better outcomes for patients. For Amgen, this collaboration represents more than a single video. It is an opportunity to introduce millions of people to the role scientific research plays in improving patients' lives, while helping a broader audience understand who Amgen is, what we do, and why continued investment in research matters. "Research is how we turn hope into something real for patients," Jay Bradner, Amgen's EVP of R&D, AI&D, said while filming with Donaldson. "Every breakthrough brings us closer to changing what's possible for children and families facing cancer." The Stand Up To Cancer Pediatric Cancer Dream Team will bring together scientists and physicians working across institutions to accelerate pediatric cancer research with one shared goal: advancing discoveries with the potential to improve outcomes for children and families facing cancer. William Yank's Story Also joining Donaldson and Bradner on camera, William Yank was diagnosed with B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia at 21. Like many young people facing cancer, his life suddenly became a series of treatments, hospital visits, and uncertainty. Today, William is living beyond cancer, advocating for other patients, and looking toward the future. In the MrBeast video, he shares how research shaped his own journey, and why continued scientific discovery offers hope for future patients and families. His story is a reminder that every breakthrough begins long before it reaches a patient. MrBeast's newest video dropped on Saturday, July 25, at 12:00 p.m. ET / 9:00 a.m. PT on YouTube. While millions will tune in for another unforgettable MrBeast production, they'll also get a closer look at the role scientific research plays in creating new possibilities for children with cancer, and the partnerships helping make that work happen. MrBeast, whose real name is Jimmy Donaldson, is the world's most-subscribed YouTube creator. He recently surpassed 500M subscribers on his YouTube channel. He is known for large-scale philanthropy and challenge videos that reach billions of viewers worldwide. Why is Amgen partnering with MrBeast? Amgen is collaborating with Stand Up To Cancer and Beast Philanthropy to help accelerate pediatric cancer research and introduce millions of people to why research matters. What is the Stand Up To Cancer Pediatric Cancer Dream Team? The Stand Up To Cancer Pediatric Cancer Dream Team will be a collaborative research project that brings together leading scientists, physicians, and institutions to accelerate discoveries for children with cancer. What does Amgen do? Amgen is a global biotechnology company focused on discovering, developing, manufacturing, and delivering innovative medicines for patients facing some of the world's most serious diseases. For more than 45 years, Amgen has invested in scientific research across oncology, cardiovascular disease, inflammation, rare diseases, and obesity. Why is a biotechnology company collaborating with MrBeast? MrBeast's audience reaches hundreds of millions of people around the world. By collaborating with Stand Up To Cancer and Beast Philanthropy, Amgen hopes to raise awareness of pediatric cancer, highlight the importance of scientific research, and inspire support for discoveries that have the potential to improve patients' lives. Why does research matter? Research is at the heart of Amgen's mission to serve patients. For more than 45 years, Amgen has invested in scientific research to better understand disease and develop innovative medicines. Every breakthrough begins with discovery, and continued research is essential to advancing new treatments for patients with serious illnesses, including cancer. Who is William Yank? William Yank is a patient advocate and social media influencer who was diagnosed with B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia at 21. Today, William is living beyond cancer and using his voice to help other patients. How can I learn more? History 1980s 1990s 2000s 2010s 2020s 1980 AMGen incorporates. AMGen (Applied Molecular Genetics Inc.) is established in Thousand Oaks, California, on April 8, 1980, as the brainchild of venture capitalists William K. (Bill) Bowes and associates. With a staff of three, the Company occupies a shared building, now called “Building 1.” Amgen has had three logos in its history. This is the first logo. 1980 George B. Rathmann is named first CEO. AMGen names its first CEO, scientist and businessman George B. Rathmann. Dubbed “Mr. Biotech” by Red Herring magazine, Rathmann has been called one of the great geniuses of high-tech entrepreneurialism. Working from a small trailer to free up space for scientists, Rathmann quickly establishes scientific goals and secures funding to conduct grand experiments in technology. George Rathmann in one of the Building 2 laboratory bays in 1982. 1980 Early experiments. In the first three years, AMGen scientists attempt many things: creating organisms to extract oil from shale, growing chickens faster, making specialty chemicals, cloning luciferase (the light source for fireflies) and creating a process for producing indigo dye in E. coli —an achievement that garners the prestigious cover of Science magazine. The final direction for the Company would be treating and curing disease. Amgen’s research in cloning genes leads to the Company's production of indigo in E. coli in the early 1980s. The discovery and subsequent patent made the cover of Science magazine in 1983. 1983 Led by CFO Gordon Binder, Amgen’s IPO on June 17, 1983, raises nearly $40 million. The Company officially changes its name to Amgen. A May 1983 article of The Wall Street Journal announces Amgen’s IPO. 1983 The clone that launched a company. A team led by a young researcher from Taiwan named Fu-Kuen Lin is tasked with finding and cloning the erythropoietin gene. Their job is staggering: finding a gene on a single fragment of DNA among 1.5 million fragments of the human genome. After working tirelessly for two years, they do it. This groundbreaking achievement enables the creation of one of the most successful drugs in biotech history, EPOGEN ® (epoetin alfa). Fu-Kuen Lin examines x-ray film to identify gene coding for erythropoietin. 1984 Kirin and Amgen form a joint venture, Kirin-Amgen, for the worldwide commercialization of erythropoietin. 1985 A second discovery. While Lin is working on erythropoietin, researcher Larry Souza and his team clone granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF). This discovery leads to the development of Amgen’s second blockbuster drug NEUPOGEN ® (filgrastim). Research head Larry Souza leads the team in the creation of NEUPOGEN ® , Amgen’s second blockbuster drug. 1988 Gordon Binder is appointed CEO. Amgen had just received the first U.S. patent for recombinant erythropoietin, completed a 20,000 page filing to the FDA for approval of EPOGEN ® (epoetin alfa) and completed building a new 24,000 square foot manufacturing facility. At this height, Rathmann announces that he is ready to retire, explaining, “I figured that would be a great thing if they got a running start by launching EPOGEN ® as the new management team.” Gordon Binder is promoted from CFO to CEO and ushers in a new and promising era. Later, the European headquarters will relocate to Zug, also in Switzerland. Today, the Amgen Foundation works to advance science education, inspire the next generation of innovators, and support communities where Amgen employees live and work. By the end of 2025, the Foundation had donated more than $500 million in grants to local, regional and international nonprofit organizations that reflect Amgen’s core values and impact lives in inspiring and innovative ways. NEUPOGEN ® is named Product of the Year by Fortune magazine. 1992 A billion-dollar company. Amgen hits $1 billion in product sales for EPOGEN ® (epoetin alfa) and NEUPOGEN ® (filgrastim) combined. On January 2, 1992, Amgen is added to the S&P 500 and months later, the Company debuts on the Fortune 500 list. Manufacturing staffers oversee a filling machine to dispense final, formulated product into vials ready for distribution. 1993 Amgen opens its Puerto Rico facility, which would become Amgen’s flagship manufacturing site with over 1.7 million square feet of space. Amgen’s profile is **a broad, cash-generative drug business with a productive growth portfolio—but one facing real patent, pricing, and debt pressures**. Based on its latest reported quarter, Q2 2026:

### Strengths
- **Diversified portfolio with several growing products.** Q2 revenue rose 10% year over year to $10.1 billion. Growth included Repatha (+37%), Evenity (+38%), Uplizna (+90%), Tezspire (+42%), and Imdelltra (+115%). That breadth helps reduce reliance on any single medicine. ([sec.gov](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/318154/000031815426000126/amgn-20260630.htm))
- **Strong commercial and research capabilities.** Amgen has a large portfolio across areas including oncology, inflammation, cardiovascular disease, and rare disease, plus experience developing and commercializing biologic medicines. Its continued R&D investment offers opportunities to refresh the portfolio, though pipeline outcomes are uncertain. ([sec.gov](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/318154/000031815426000010/amgn-20251231.htm))
- **Substantial cash generation.** It produced $3.5 billion of free cash flow in Q2 2026, supporting investment and shareholder returns. ([amgen.com](https://www.amgen.com/newsroom/press-releases/2026/08/amgen-reports-second-quarter-2026-financial-results))

### Weaknesses and risks
- **Patent losses and biosimilar competition are already biting.** In Q2, Prolia sales fell 32% and XGEVA fell 34% year over year as biosimilars gained ground. Amgen warns that patent or exclusivity losses can cause rapid sales declines. ([amgen.com](https://www.amgen.com/newsroom/press-releases/2026/08/amgen-reports-second-quarter-2026-financial-results))
- **Pricing and reimbursement pressure.** Enbrel sales fell 4% in Q2, with lower prices reflecting Medicare Part D price setting and a higher 340B mix; Otezla sales fell 21%. These examples show how policy changes and payer negotiations can offset gains in prescription volume. ([amgen.com](https://www.amgen.com/newsroom/press-releases/2026/08/amgen-reports-second-quarter-2026-financial-results))
- **Significant debt.** At June 30, 2026, Amgen reported $57.3 billion of debt and $14.0 billion of cash. Its cash flow is strong, but that debt load limits flexibility and makes successful integration of acquisitions and steady earnings important. ([amgen.com](https://www.amgen.com/newsroom/press-releases/2026/08/amgen-reports-second-quarter-2026-financial-results))
- **Drug development remains uncertain.** Heavy R&D spending does not guarantee that candidates will succeed in trials, receive approval, or become major sellers; Amgen identifies these as risks in its filings. ([sec.gov](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/318154/000031815426000010/amgn-20251231.htm))

**Bottom line:** Amgen’s strongest assets are its scale, breadth of marketed medicines, and ability to generate cash. The central challenge is replacing revenue from older products losing exclusivity while sustaining growth without letting pricing pressure, R&D risk, or debt weigh too heavily.

**Assuming you mean Amgen (AMGN) as a stock:** I’d consider it a **reasonable long-term holding, but not an automatic buy at any price**. Whether it suits you depends on your time horizon, risk tolerance, and existing portfolio.

**Why I’d consider it**
- The business is growing: in Q2 2026, revenue rose **10% year over year to $10.1 billion**, and management raised its full-year revenue and adjusted-EPS outlook. Several products—including Repatha and Tezspire—posted strong sales growth. ([amgen.com](https://www.amgen.com/newsroom/press-releases/2026/08/amgen-reports-second-quarter-2026-financial-results))
- It has a broad portfolio and substantial cash generation: Q2 free cash flow was **$3.5 billion**. That can support investment in new medicines and dividends. ([amgen.com](https://www.amgen.com/newsroom/press-releases/2026/08/amgen-reports-second-quarter-2026-financial-results))
- At the latest quote available to me—about **$410 on September 22, 2026**—the stock is roughly **18× the midpoint of management’s 2026 adjusted-EPS guidance**. That’s not an obviously cheap valuation, but it may be acceptable to an investor who believes growth will continue. ([amgen.com](https://www.amgen.com/newsroom/press-releases/2026/08/amgen-reports-second-quarter-2026-financial-results))

**Why I’d be cautious**
- Some established products face real erosion: Q2 sales of Prolia fell **32%** year over year, with biosimilar competition also weighing on Xgeva. ([amgen.com](https://www.amgen.com/newsroom/press-releases/2026/08/amgen-reports-second-quarter-2026-financial-results))
- The company had **$57.3 billion in debt** and $14.0 billion in cash at June 30, 2026. That debt is manageable only if cash flows and the portfolio hold up. ([amgen.com](https://www.amgen.com/newsroom/press-releases/2026/08/amgen-reports-second-quarter-2026-financial-results))
- Like any drugmaker, it faces clinical-trial, regulatory, pricing, litigation, and patent risks; its future growth depends partly on newer medicines and pipeline programs succeeding. ([amgen.com](https://www.amgen.com/newsroom/press-releases/2026/08/amgen-reports-second-quarter-2026-financial-results))

**Bottom line:** I’d lean **“consider it, preferably at a sensible valuation and as part of a diversified portfolio,”** especially for someone seeking exposure to a large biotech company with established cash flows. I wouldn’t buy it solely for the dividend or treat it as a low-risk investment. This is a general view, not personalized financial advice.

**From September 22, 2025 through September 22, 2026**, Amgen’s biggest changes were faster growth in several newer medicines, an expanded pipeline, and a major regulatory dispute over TAVNEOS.

- **The business grew, but performance varied across products.** For 2025, revenue rose 10% to **$36.8 billion**. In Q2 2026, revenue was **$10.1 billion, up 10% year over year**, and Amgen forecast full-year 2026 revenue of **$38.2–$39.4 billion**. Growth leaders included Repatha, UPLIZNA, TEZSPIRE and IMDELLTRA. Meanwhile, biosimilar competition pushed Q2 sales of Prolia down 32% and XGEVA down 34% year over year. ([amgen.com](https://www.amgen.com/newsroom/press-releases/2026/02/amgen-reports-fourth-quarter-and-full-year-2025-financial-results))

- **Its pipeline is advancing on obesity and cancer.** Amgen’s obesity drug candidate MariTide is now being tested in multiple Phase 3 studies, including weight management, cardiovascular outcomes and sleep apnea. In September 2026, Amgen also reported that a Phase 3 trial of cancer drug IMDELLTRA plus AstraZeneca’s Imfinzi improved overall survival versus Imfinzi alone in first-line maintenance treatment for extensive-stage small-cell lung cancer; the detailed results have not yet been presented. ([amgen.com](https://www.amgen.com/newsroom/press-releases/2026/08/amgen-reports-second-quarter-2026-financial-results))

- **It added assets and broadened some medicines’ reach.** Amgen bought UK biotech Dark Blue Therapeutics in January for up to **$840 million**, adding an early-stage leukemia drug program. In Europe, UPLIZNA gained approval for generalized myasthenia gravis, and IMDYLLTRA was approved for extensive-stage small-cell lung cancer. ([amgen.com](https://www.amgen.com/newsroom/press-releases/2026/01/amgen-acquires-dark-blue-therapeutics-bolstering-oncology-pipeline))

- **TAVNEOS became a significant regulatory risk.** In April 2026, the FDA proposed withdrawing the drug, saying it had not been shown effective for its approved use and that the original application contained untrue statements of material fact. Amgen disputes the proposal and sought a hearing; as of the latest company update, the drug remained on the U.S. market while the process continued. ([fda.gov](https://www.fda.gov/drugs/drug-alerts-and-statements/cder-proposes-withdraw-approval-tavneos?utm_source=openai))

- **Leadership and manufacturing changed too.** Amgen appointed Thomas Dittrich CFO effective September 1, 2026, replacing retiring CFO Peter Griffith. It also reorganized senior roles to bring R&D, AI and data closer together, and announced nearly **$2 billion in U.S. manufacturing investments over the preceding year**. ([amgen.com](https://www.amgen.com/newsroom/press-releases/2026/05/amgen-announces-retirement-of-chief-financial-officer-peter-griffith))

**Bottom line:** Amgen has stronger momentum in several growth products and a busier late-stage pipeline, particularly in obesity and oncology. The main counterweights are competition eroding some established drug sales and uncertainty around TAVNEOS.

**Short version:** Amgen is the smallest of the four by revenue, but it grew fastest in 2025. It’s a biotech-focused company with a broadening portfolio. Novartis is a focused global medicines company; Pfizer is broader and larger, with vaccines and a major oncology business; Merck & Co. is also larger, but its sales are especially dependent on Keytruda.

### At a glance

| Company | 2025 revenue | Q2 2026 revenue growth* | Business profile |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| **Amgen** | **$36.8B**; +10% | **$10.1B**; +10% | Biologics-heavy portfolio spanning cardiovascular, bone health, inflammation, cancer and rare diseases. Repatha, Prolia and several rare-disease medicines are key products. ([amgen.com](https://www.amgen.com/stories/2026/03/2025-letter-to-shareholders?utm_source=openai)) |
| **Novartis** | **$54.5B**; +8% | **$14.4B**; +3% reported, +1% at constant currency | “Pure-play” innovative medicines company, with major franchises in oncology, immunology, neuroscience and cardiovascular/renal/metabolic disease. Recent growth drivers include Kisqali, Kesimpta and Pluvicto. ([novartis.com](https://www.novartis.com/investors/financial-data/annual-results?utm_source=openai)) |
| **Pfizer** | **$62.6B**; −2% operationally | **$15.0B**; +3% reported, +1% operationally | Broad pharma and vaccine business, including oncology, vaccines and cardiovascular medicines. Pfizer said its launched and acquired products grew 18% operationally in Q2, while overall revenue grew more slowly. ([annualreview.pfizer.com](https://annualreview.pfizer.com/?utm_source=openai)) |
| **Merck & Co.** | **$65.0B**; +1% | **$16.6B**; +5% reported, +4% excluding currency | Strong in oncology, vaccines and animal health. Keytruda is its dominant product: 2025 sales were **$31.7B**, nearly half of company revenue. ([merck.com](https://www.merck.com/stories/our-q4-and-full-year-2025-financial-results/?utm_source=openai)) |

\*Q2 2026 growth rates are company-reported; “operational” or “constant currency” excludes foreign-exchange effects, so the percentages are not perfectly identical measures.

### What distinguishes Amgen

- **More focused, smaller scale:** Amgen’s 2025 revenue was roughly half Novartis’s and somewhat more than half Pfizer’s or Merck’s. But its 10% growth was stronger than the others’ in that year. Amgen said 14 products each generated over $1B in 2025, so it isn’t reliant on just one blockbuster. ([amgen.com](https://www.amgen.com/stories/2026/03/2025-letter-to-shareholders?utm_source=openai))
- **Its growth is coming from a mix of established and newer franchises:** Repatha sales rose 36% in 2025 to $3.0B, while products added through the Horizon acquisition broadened Amgen’s rare-disease business. One counterweight is Prolia: Amgen expects more sales erosion as biosimilar competition expands. ([investors.amgen.com](https://investors.amgen.com/news-releases/news-release-details/amgen-reports-fourth-quarter-and-full-year-2025-financial?utm_source=openai))
- **The others have different concentration risks:** Merck has the most obvious single-product dependence, with Keytruda at $31.7B in 2025. Pfizer’s top 10 medicines and vaccines made up 61% of revenue in 2025, though that revenue was spread across several products. Novartis’s recent growth has been driven by several newer medicines, while generic competition is pressuring products such as Entresto. ([merck.com](https://www.merck.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/124/2026/02/4Q25-Merck-Earnings-Announcement.pdf?utm_source=openai))

**Bottom line:** Amgen stands out for its 2025 growth and biotech-centered portfolio, but it is smaller than the other three. Novartis looks more like a focused global innovative-medicines company; Pfizer offers broader scale and a wide product mix; Merck has the greatest dependence on a single blockbuster. This is a business comparison, not a valuation or stock-pick comparison.

In the U.S., start with the **doctor treating the illness**—often a specialist such as an oncologist, rheumatologist, or gastroenterologist. They can determine whether a biologic is appropriate and arrange access through:

- **A hospital or infusion center** if the medicine is given by infusion or injection there.
- **A specialty pharmacy** if it’s prescribed for use at home. Your doctor or insurer can tell you which pharmacy is in-network. ([fda.gov](https://www.fda.gov/drugs/biosimilars/biosimilars-basics-patients?utm_source=openai))

Ask the doctor’s office or your health insurer about **FDA-approved biosimilar options**, which may be covered or cost less for some medicines. ([fda.gov](https://www.fda.gov/drugs/biosimilars/biosimilars-basics-patients?utm_source=openai)) If cost is a barrier, ask the clinic’s social worker or pharmacist about financial-assistance options.

If you mean an **experimental biologic**, ask the specialist about a clinical trial or FDA expanded access; expanded access is arranged with a licensed physician and is not a direct-purchase route. ([fda.gov](https://www.fda.gov/news-events/expanded-access/expanded-access-information-patients?utm_source=openai))

Avoid buying biologics from social media or websites that don’t require a prescription. FDA advises checking that an online pharmacy is licensed and has a U.S. address and pharmacist. ([fda.gov](https://www.fda.gov/consumers/consumer-updates/how-buy-medicines-safely-online-pharmacy?utm_source=openai))

In the **U.S.**, start with the specialist treating the illness. Biologic medicines usually require a prescription, and the right place to get one depends on the specific medicine:

- **Specialty pharmacy:** Many biologics are delivered by a specialty pharmacy, sometimes to your home or clinic.
- **Infusion center or hospital clinic:** Some must be given by a healthcare professional. Your prescriber can identify an appropriate site.
- **Your insurer or pharmacist:** Ask which specialty pharmacy or infusion center is in-network and whether the medicine needs prior authorization. Medicare coverage can differ depending on where and how a drug is given. ([medicare.gov](https://www.medicare.gov/coverage/prescription-drugs-outpatient?utm_source=openai))

If cost is a concern, ask the prescriber’s office or pharmacist about an FDA-approved **biosimilar** alternative and manufacturer assistance programs. Avoid buying biologics from unverified websites; check that any online pharmacy is licensed in your state. ([fda.gov](https://www.fda.gov/ForConsumers/ConsumerUpdates/ucm436399.htm?utm_source=openai))

If you mean an **experimental** biologic because standard treatments aren’t suitable, ask your specialist about clinical trials or FDA expanded access; eligibility and access aren’t guaranteed. ([clinicaltrials.gov](https://clinicaltrials.gov/find-studies/for-patients/how-to-join?utm_source=openai))

If you share your **illness, state or ZIP code, and whether you have insurance**, I can help narrow down where to start.

points.name: Amgen
sentences: **Amgen** is a biotechnology company that discovers, develops, and manufactures medicines.
Its treatments address serious illnesses in areas such as cancer, inflammation, rare diseases, and general medicine.

([amgen.com](https://www.amgen.com/about?utm_source=openai))

It’s **for patients who have conditions that an Amgen medicine is approved to treat**, and for the healthcare professionals who prescribe and manage those treatments.
It isn’t a healthcare provider or a medicine for one particular condition; whether an Amgen drug is appropriate depends on someone’s diagnosis and should be discussed with their clinician.

**Amgen is a biotechnology company that discovers and makes medicines for serious diseases.** In simple terms, it uses biology and science to develop treatments—especially for cancer, rare diseases, inflammation, and common conditions.
It’s one of the companies behind medicines patients may receive through their doctors.

([amgen.com](https://www.amgen.com/about?utm_source=openai))

A simple comparison: **it’s like a pharmaceutical company with a strong focus on medicines developed using biotechnology.**
Amgen is best known as a **pioneer in biotechnology**—a company that develops biologic medicines for serious illnesses.
Its early landmark drugs included **Epogen** for anemia related to chronic kidney disease and **Neupogen** to help patients recover white blood cells after chemotherapy.

([amgen.com](https://www.amgen.com/about/amgen-history?utm_source=openai))

Today, Amgen works across areas including cancer, inflammation, rare diseases, and general medicine.
Well-known medicines include **Enbrel**, **Repatha**, and **Prolia**.
Amgen’s profile is **a broad, cash-generative drug business with a productive growth portfolio—but one facing real patent, pricing, and debt pressures**.

Based on its latest reported quarter, Q2 2026:

### Strengths
- **Diversified portfolio with several growing products.** Q2 revenue rose 10% year over year to $10.1 billion.
Growth included Repatha (+37%), Evenity (+38%), Uplizna (+90%), Tezspire (+42%), and Imdelltra (+115%).
That breadth helps reduce reliance on any single medicine.

([sec.gov](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/318154/000031815426000126/amgn-20260630.htm))
- **Strong commercial and research capabilities.** Amgen has a large portfolio across areas including oncology, inflammation, cardiovascular disease, and rare disease, plus experience developing and commercializing biologic medicines.
Its continued R&D investment offers opportunities to refresh the portfolio, though pipeline outcomes are uncertain.

([sec.gov](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/318154/000031815426000010/amgn-20251231.htm))
- **Substantial cash generation.** It produced $3.5 billion of free cash flow in Q2 2026, supporting investment and shareholder returns.

([amgen.com](https://www.amgen.com/newsroom/press-releases/2026/08/amgen-reports-second-quarter-2026-financial-results))

### Weaknesses and risks
- **Patent losses and biosimilar competition are already biting.** In Q2, Prolia sales fell 32% and XGEVA fell 34% year over year as biosimilars gained ground.
Amgen warns that patent or exclusivity losses can cause rapid sales declines.
